query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing 5–10 wt% aluminum into a refractory high-entropy alloy will promote the in situ formation of a continuous, adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale during high-temperature exposure, thereby substantially reducing oxidation compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy that lacks significant aluminum content and exhibits poor oxygen resistance when exposed to extreme temperatures.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition to include an additional 5–10 wt% aluminum.
generation.conditions: Exposure at approximately 1100 °C in ambient air (high oxygen partial pressure) for up to 100 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dense, adherent alumina scale on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the added aluminum diffuses to the surface and oxidizes, forming a protective Al2O3 layer that acts as a barrier to oxygen ingress. This reduces further oxidation of the underlying alloy, thereby improving its overall oxygen resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the Al-doped alloy is expected to show a significantly lower oxidation weight gain and a well-formed, continuous alumina scale, indicating enhanced oxygen resistance.
generation.baseline: The untreated refractory high-entropy alloy which, under the same high-temperature exposure conditions, exhibits a higher oxidation rate and less protective oxide formation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is confined to high-temperature (≈1100 °C), high oxygen partial pressure environments, and may not hold under significantly different temperatures or atmospheres. Additionally, while oxygen resistance is improved, any impact on other mechanical properties is not addressed.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal aluminum content for balancing oxidation resistance and maintaining other mechanical properties is uncertain, as is the scalability of this effect over longer exposure times or under cyclic thermal conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples: one set of the baseline refractory high-entropy alloy and one set modified with 5–10 wt% added aluminum. Subject both sets to a controlled oxidation test at 1100 °C in ambient air for 100 hours. After exposure, perform weight-gain analysis and use surface characterization techniques (e.g., SEM/EDS and XRD) to examine the oxide scale formation.
measurements: Phase composition of the oxide scale via XRD and elemental mapping via SEM/EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped alloy does not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in oxidation weight gain and fails to form a continuous, protective alumina scale compared to the untreated alloy, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
